elements.element: Preferred: Customer owns deliverables/work product created for it, with Vendor assignment
elements.evidence: "Any writing or work of authorship created by M&I ... even if paid for by Customer, shall be the property of M&I"; no assignment added
"All programs (including ideas and know-how and concepts) developed by M&I are and shall remain M&I's sole property."

elements.element: Preferred: perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free licence to Vendor IP embedded in deliverables
elements.evidence: inserted licence covers "the Developed Software", not Vendor IP embedded in Customer-owned deliverables

elements.element: Preferred: Customer retains all rights in Customer Data
elements.evidence: no operative Customer Data ownership language in clause or insertion
no joint-ownership language present or expressly excluded
"M&I owns its generic tools and know-how"
"the Developed Software" — the defined output of "[a]ny writing or work of authorship created by M&I in the course of performing the Services"

elements.element: Fallback: scope is for Customer's business

reasons: The single inserted sentence completes every atomic element of the fallback: Vendor retention of generic tools and know-how plus a perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide, royalty-free licence to use, modify and sublicense the Developed Software for Customer's business.
Preferred is not met (no assignment of deliverables, no embedded-Vendor-IP licence, no Customer Data retention, no express no-joint-ownership), which is consistent with the locked fallback target.
Minimality holds: one concise insertion for an absent licence, no rewrite of ownership language, and 10.4's refund/credit mechanic is untouched.

Intent preserved: no undefined terms introduced ('Developed Software' is defined in 10.4); 17.2's limitation on M&I systems addresses M&I-provided software rather than the licensed Developed Software, so no operative contradiction, though noting the interaction in the rationale would be prudent.
